Boring Stocks Are Beautiful Again. Can It Last?
 
Plus, all eyes on these hyperscalers
 

It’s Fed Day, but it’s highly unlikely that the central bank will be making headlines this afternoon so close to U.S. midterm elections. Instead, the attention will be on “hyperscalers” Microsoft and Alphabet, which report quarterly results a couple of hours later. Investors responded unenthusiastically to Meta’s big spending plans last week. Stock futures are mixed ahead of the bell and oil is up overnight on news of potential U.S. plans to resume attacks on Iran.

 

​📈 Follow our live markets data and coverage.

Slow and steady wins the race

 

Here’s some not-very-exciting news for you: The glitzy stocks that have carried the baton for this bull market sputtered this month.

 

But investors who embraced stodgier ones are having a great October. Whether or not the coming weeks or months look the same, they seem to have the right idea.

 

From last April’s Liberation Day low through the end of September, a basket of high-beta (volatile) stocks in the S&P 500 trounced the index’s least-volatile components. They rose 121 percentage points more—a stunning result.

 

But that pattern has flipped. The low-volatility group has outperformed the racier one by 13 percentage points over four weeks. Other S&P 500 subsectors that were laggards have had a bumper month too, including Dividend Aristocrats and Pure Value. Standout stocks include Berkshire Hathaway, Duke Energy, Aflac, Tyson Foods, Chevron, Procter & Gamble and Costco.

 

We’ve seen this movie before. Times when the stock market has a big scare that resolves quickly seem to inspire exceptional risk-taking behavior once the smoke clears.

 

Two similar periods to the post-Liberation Day bounce are the ones after hedge fund Long Term Capital Management had to be rescued in 1998 and the Covid panic in 2020. The main danger at such times, especially for professional fund managers being evaluated against a benchmark, is taking too little risk.

 

In both cases, the effect lasted 20 months or so. What used to be called “old economy” stocks get left out of the party and get relatively cheap compared to the overall market. 

 

That sets the stage for a strong comeback. It would be an investor’s dream to get the timing right, but even being early has worked out. Owning the least volatile decile of U.S. stocks over the entire 1998-2003 period, for example, made an investor the most money despite a tech rally until March 2000. 

 

Volatility subindexes haven’t existed that long, but fund managers who have studied the so-called “Low Beta Anomaly” have shown that entire decades—the 1930s, 1970s and 2000s—were good times to own boring stocks.

 

There’s a catch, though—that’s just relative to the market. They were still trying times to own stocks in general. 

 

Each of those decades followed rip-roaring bull markets and saw public participation in the stock market fall sharply from high levels. A famous 1979 Business Week cover story proclaimed “The Death of Equities,” for example. 

 

With the benefit of hindsight, we know that the market came back eventually and that staying invested was the smart move. It’s a bit easier, not to mention more profitable, when owning stocks that tend to lose less and to do best over an entire cycle.

 

It might be early to trim bets on today’s most-exciting story, the AI boom, but history tells us it can help keep you in the game.
